paper.abstract: Abstract The flat voltage plateau of lithium iron phosphate (LFP)/graphite cells makes electrochemical-state errors and voltage-measurement abnormalities produce similar innovations, complicating state-of-charge (SOC) estimation. This work proposes an electrochemically constrained residual-bias compensation dual extended Kalman filter (RBC-DEKF) with uncertain-initialization commissioning. A thermal control-oriented parameter-grouped single-particle model (CPG-SPMT) provides paired-electrode dynamics and terminal-voltage prediction, while a separately configurable voltage-discrepancy state accommodates systematic residuals. When the initial SOC is uncertain, residual adaptation is suspended over a verified-healthy startup window. Buffered data support electrochemically constrained trajectory matching, followed by calibrated state replay and residual-channel reactivation. Frozen cross-cycle healthy-residual calibration supports commissioning and remains in the voltage prediction after handover. Evaluation covers 216 additive-bias and 168 multiplicative-gain profiles over 24 A123 temperature–drive-cycle trajectories. Relative to Single-EKF, the original RBC-DEKF reduces mean SOC RMSE from 7.646 to 0.170 percentage points for additive bias and from 22.646 to 0.356 percentage points for gain faults. Separately, 18 nonzero-initial-error profiles on three representative 50%-SOC-anchored segments give a full-record mean SOC RMSE of 1.747 percentage points, including startup, for the commissioned realization, versus 11.192 and 11.400 for the always-on RBC-DEKF and conventional joint EKF. Representative delayed bias, 10-s ramp, and gain tests show that the corrected SOC trajectory remains stable after fault introduction. The central contribution is electrochemically constrained temporal coordination of uncertain-state recovery and subsequent voltage-discrepancy accommodation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) has become one of the most widely deployed cathode materials in lithium-ion batteries for electric transportation and stationary energy-storage applications, owing to its intrinsic safety, long cycle life, thermal stability, and cost-effectiveness [ 28 , 25 , 16 ] . Despite these advantages, reliable state estimation remains particularly challenging for LFP batteries [ 23 , 41 ] . Lithium insertion and extraction proceed through a two-phase reaction between Li-rich LiFePO 4 and Li-poor FePO 4 , producing an extended and nearly flat open-circuit-voltage (OCV) plateau over a broad state-of-charge (SOC) range [ 6 , 51 ] . Within this plateau, the terminal voltage changes only weakly with SOC, substantially reducing voltage-based state observability [ 24 , 51 ] . Consequently, a small voltage uncertainty can correspond to a large SOC ambiguity, making voltage-corrected SOC estimation intrinsically more difficult for LFP batteries than for chemistries with steeper OCV–SOC characteristics. This weak observability places stringent requirements on the accuracy and reliability of voltage measurements used by battery management systems (BMSs) [ 27 , 32 , 4 , 51 ] . In long-term operation, however, voltage sensors may suffer from calibration drift, reference instability, component aging, and environmental influences [ 53 , 37 , 48 , 34 ] , with recent studies further emphasizing sensor-enabled monitoring under extreme environments and coupled thermal–electrical aging stresses [ 42 , 36 ] . These abnormalities commonly appear as additive offsets at the millivolt level or as multiplicative gain errors that rescale the measured voltage [ 54 ] . In an LFP battery, such apparently small sensing errors can be mapped onto disproportionately large corrections of the weakly observable electrochemical states, leading to severe SOC-estimation degradation or loss of convergence. Since SOC is a central variable for power limitation, energy management, balancing, and safety supervision, the resulting error can propagate through multiple BMS functions and compromise system-level reliability [ 31 , 46 ] . Voltage-sensor robustness is therefore not merely an instrumentation issue, but a material-dependent state-estimation problem for flat-plateau LFP batteries. Battery fault-diagnosis methods are commonly divided into signal-processing-based, data-driven, and model-based approaches. Signal-processing methods extract abnormal temporal or spectral features directly from measurements and are attractive because of their relatively simple implementation [ 50 , 47 ] . Their performance, however, can be sensitive to measurement noise, operating-condition variation, and the choice of diagnostic thresholds. Data-driven methods have demonstrated strong nonlinear representation capability for voltage-abnormality detection and battery fault classification [ 56 , 20 , 21 ] , but generally require representative fault data and may exhibit limited generalization to previously unseen cells, temperatures, and load profiles [ 55 , 18 , 43 ] . Recent realistic and model-constrained learning studies have improved fault diagnosis under stochastic and heterogeneous operating conditions [ 49 , 2 ] ; nevertheless, transferring laboratory-trained diagnosis models to practical battery systems remains difficult because of changing operating distributions, sensing limitations, and multi-scale fault manifestations [ 55 ] . Model-based approaches provide an alternative route by linking faults to the inconsistency between measured and model-predicted battery responses [ 44 , 5 ] ; structural residual analysis has also been developed to isolate concurrent electro–thermal faults in battery systems [ 33 ] . Most existing methods employ equivalent circuit models (ECMs), whose low computational cost and simple calibration are attractive for online BMS implementation. However, their residuals combine sensor abnormalities with process disturbances, parameter errors, and structural model mismatch, which complicates fault interpretation and threshold design [ 44 ] . This problem is particularly severe for LFP batteries: within the flat OCV region, a persistent voltage residual can be incorrectly explained by a large change in SOC even when the actual source is a sensor fault or modeling error. Electrochemical models offer a more physically consistent basis for separating voltage formation from internal-state evolution. The pseudo-two-dimensional model and its reduced-order variants explicitly represent lithium transport, interfacial kinetics, and electrode thermodynamics, thereby connecting terminal voltage to physically meaningful internal states [ 7 , 15 ] . Although the full-order model is generally too computationally demanding for recursive onboard estimation, reduced-order models such as the single-particle model preserve the dominant electrochemical dynamics at substantially lower computational cost [ 12 , 8 ] . A direct comparison on graphite/LFP cells reported an average voltage-prediction error of 51.5 mV for an ECM and 19.3 mV for a physics-based model over temperatures of 10–40 ∘ C and rates of C/3–2C, illustrating the value of electrochemical descriptions for LFP voltage prediction [ 19 ] . Residual correction provides an additional mechanism for addressing the discrepancy that remains even with a physics-based model. Physics-guided residual-learning frameworks have shown that an electrochemical-model prior can be combined with learned correction terms to improve LFP SOC estimation over broad temperature ranges and dynamic operating conditions [ 10 , 3 ] . These studies demonstrate that model residuals contain useful information for correcting state estimates. However, learned residual models generally require representative offline training data and primarily target model-induced prediction errors. They do not explicitly formulate voltage-sensor bias and gain abnormalities within the measurement model or recursively estimate a voltage-discrepancy state for online accommodation of both fault forms. Several fault-tolerant strategies more directly related to voltage measurements have also been investigated. Sensor-topology-based reconstruction can tolerate isolated voltage-sensor faults by exploiting redundant pack measurements [ 38 ] , but its applicability depends on measurement redundancy and fault configuration. Adaptive filtering can improve robustness against small voltage perturbations [ 22 ] , although such perturbations are often treated as generic uncertainty rather than explicit sensor faults. For LFP batteries, region-dependent methods have adjusted the correction strategy according to the local OCV slope or selected different observers for different OCV ranges [ 40 , 26 ] . Bias-compensated SOC and state-of-health estimation has also been developed by exploiting transitions between OCV regions [ 45 ] . These approaches improve estimation within flat-voltage regions, but typically require SOC-region identification, observer switching, or convergence across multiple charge–discharge intervals. In parallel, additive bias and multiplicative gain faults have been jointly represented through state augmentation in ECM-based estimators [ 54 ] . Their performance nevertheless remains strongly dependent on model fidelity and excitation, while the interaction between voltage-sensor abnormalities and the material-specific weak observability of LFP electrochemical states has not been explicitly addressed. Incorrect SOC initialization has been addressed through several complementary estimation strategies. Closed-loop UKF estimation has demonstrated self-correction from a large initial offset in an LFP cell [ 17 ] , while nonlinear observers have provided convergence analysis and recovery tests under a 20-percentage-point initial error [ 39 ] . Moving-horizon estimation exploits a finite measurement history and physical constraints to reduce sensitivity to mismatched initial conditions [ 29 , 30 ] , and adaptive robust filters improve convergence when the initial SOC, model parameters, and noise statistics are simultaneously uncertain [ 35 ] . These studies demonstrate the value of temporal excitation and constrained state evolution for recovering an uncertain SOC prior. Staged adaptation has also been used in battery state–parameter co-estimation. Voltage-error dead zones can temporarily suspend physical-parameter updates when the innovation is unsuitable for reliable adaptation, including during large SOC-initialization errors [ 14 ] . Such methods primarily regulate physical quantities such as capacity, impedance, or OCV-related coefficients. In the present fault-tolerant setting, the auxiliary state instead represents a voltage-domain discrepancy that must remain available for subsequent voltage-abnormality accommodation. Without a dedicated startup allocation strategy, this rapidly adaptive residual state can absorb an initial electrochemical-state mismatch and prevent SOC recovery. These studies highlight a central design challenge: on the flat LFP plateau, electrochemical-state error, model discrepancy, and sensor abnormality can produce similar voltage innovations. A fault-tolerant estimator must therefore coordinate state recovery and voltage-discrepancy accommodation without allowing a rapidly adaptive residual state to absorb uncertain initialization. Motivated by these considerations, this work develops an electrochemically constrained, commissioning-enabled fault-tolerant SOC-estimation framework for flat-plateau LFP batteries. The main contributions are threefold: 1. Material-specific fault sensitivity. The voltage-error sensitivity of LFP SOC estimation is quantified by linking the flat full-cell OCV response with the paired-electrode electrochemical description. This establishes the material-level motivation for explicitly accommodating systematic voltage discrepancy in flat-plateau state estimation. 2. Commissioning-enabled state–residual coordination. A sequential residual-bias compensation dual extended Kalman filter (RBC-DEKF) is developed with separately configurable electrochemical-state and voltage-discrepancy recursions. Under uncertain initialization, residual adaptation is temporarily suspended while an electrochemically consistent paired-electrode state is corrected from a verified-healthy buffered startup trajectory, after which residual accommodation is reactivated. 3. Systematic evaluation and operating-boundary analysis. Additive-bias and multiplicative-gain accommodation is evaluated over 24 temperature–drive-cycle trajectories, with separate representative tests of large initial-SOC errors and abnormalities introduced during operation. Comparisons with Single-EKF, open-loop propagation, and conventional joint augmentation distinguish fault accommodation from model propagation and state-recovery capability.

sections.heading: 2.2 Control-oriented parameter-grouped electrochemical model

sections.heading: 3 Electrochemically constrained fault-tolerant state estimation
sections.text: This section presents the proposed fault-tolerant state-estimation framework built upon the CPG-SPMT in Section 2.2 and the material-specific voltage sensitivity discussed in Section 2.3. The electrochemical states are constrained by lithium-transport dynamics in the positive and negative particles, whereas the dominant systematic voltage mismatch is represented by a separate scalar voltage-discrepancy state. This separation is an estimator design choice that allocates adaptation between two physically different roles; it neither adds an independent measurement nor removes the intrinsic weak observability of the LFP plateau. Figure 2 summarizes the operating conditions, electrochemical model, voltage abnormalities, commissioning-enabled RBC-DEKF, and expanded validation matrix. The state-first sequential recursion is specified in Section 3.2, and the commissioning procedure and comparison estimators are defined in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 , respectively. sections.heading: 3.1 Problem formulation and measurement model
sections.text: The objective of this work is to achieve accurate and fault-tolerant battery state estimation in the presence of abnormal voltage measurements (see Figure 2 (c)). The corresponding fault-tolerant estimation architecture is illustrated in Figure 2 (e). Let z k z_{k} denote the measured terminal voltage at sample k k , and let h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k}) denote the nonlinear terminal-voltage output predicted by the electrochemical model introduced in Section 2.2, where 𝐱 k \mathbf{x}_{k} is the model state, I k I_{k} is the applied current, and T k T_{k} is the cell temperature. In practice, the electrochemical model is only an approximation of the true battery behavior. Therefore, the true terminal voltage can be written as V k true = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + δ k model , V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}, (16) where δ k model \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}} denotes the systematic voltage deviation caused by model mismatch, parameter uncertainty, temperature-dependent approximation error, and other unmodeled effects. Under healthy sensing conditions, the measured voltage is then expressed as z k = V k true + v k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + δ k model + v k , z_{k}=V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}+v_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}+v_{k}, (17) where v k v_{k} denotes measurement noise. In this study, two representative abnormal measurement modes are considered. The first is an additive bias fault, represented as an additive voltage-domain offset: z k = V k true + V bias , k + v k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + δ k model + V bias , k + v k . z_{k}=V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}+V_{\mathrm{bias},k}+v_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}+V_{\mathrm{bias},k}+v_{k}. (18) The second is a multiplicative gain fault: z k = ( 1 + α ) ​ V k true + v k = ( 1 + α ) ​ ( h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + δ k model ) + v k , z_{k}=(1+\alpha)\,V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}+v_{k}=(1+\alpha)\big(h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}\big)+v_{k}, (19) where α \alpha is the gain-fault coefficient. Equation ( 19 ) can be equivalently rewritten as z k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + δ k model + α ​ V k true + v k , z_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}+\alpha V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}+v_{k}, (20) which shows that a gain fault can be represented in the voltage-residual domain by the scalar, time-varying term α ​ V k true \alpha V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}} . Although the underlying sensor abnormality is multiplicative, its instantaneous voltage contribution is scalar. The residual state can therefore represent the combined discrepancy containing the gain-induced term without explicitly identifying α \alpha . Compared with a constant additive offset, the adaptation demand increases when that combined residual becomes larger or varies more rapidly with terminal voltage. Equations ( 18 )–( 20 ) also indicate that the systematic voltage residual generally contains two coupled sources: model-induced voltage mismatch δ k model \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{model}} and sensor-induced measurement abnormality. As a result, the compensation term estimated later in this work should be interpreted as a lumped voltage-discrepancy term rather than a pure sensor-bias estimate. The discrete-time state equation of the control-oriented electrochemical model is written as 𝐱 k = A d ​ ( T k ) ​ 𝐱 k − 1 + B d ​ ( T k ) ​ I k + 𝐰 k , \mathbf{x}_{k}=A_{d}(T_{k})\mathbf{x}_{k-1}+B_{d}(T_{k})I_{k}+\mathbf{w}_{k}, (21) Here k k indexes a processed data row: the implementation propagates the previous state using that row’s I k , T k I_{k},T_{k} , then evaluates its voltage against z k z_{k} . The initial checkpoint precedes row k = 0 k=0 and is denoted 𝐱 − 1 \mathbf{x}_{-1} in this sampled recursion. The matrices A d ​ ( ⋅ ) A_{d}(\cdot) and B d ​ ( ⋅ ) B_{d}(\cdot) are the temperature-dependent discrete-time system matrices obtained by zero-order hold discretization, and 𝐰 k \mathbf{w}_{k} is the process noise. The state vector contains the reduced diffusion states of the positive and negative electrodes, from which the cell SOC is calculated as described in Section 2.2. The above formulation defines the abnormal voltage measurement modes considered in this work, while the specific injected fault levels used for experimental evaluation are introduced in Section 3.7 . Locally, the voltage innovation can be approximated as ν k ≃ H x , k ​ δ ​ 𝐱 k + δ ​ θ k + v k . \nu_{k}\simeq H_{x,k}\,\delta\mathbf{x}_{k}+\delta\theta_{k}+v_{k}. (22) Equation ( 22 ) makes the central ambiguity explicit: one scalar innovation cannot, in general, uniquely attribute a persistent discrepancy to electrochemical-state error, sensor abnormality, unmodeled hysteresis, or other model error. The following architectures impose different dynamic and covariance structures on that allocation, but do not create new measurement information.

sections.heading: 3.2 Residual-bias compensation dual extended Kalman filter (RBC-DEKF) framework
sections.text: To improve robustness against abnormal voltage measurements, an electrochemically constrained fault-tolerant estimation paradigm is developed based on the model and sensitivity structure introduced in Section 2. The proposed framework starts from a conventional extended Kalman filter (EKF) for state estimation and augments it with an online residual-bias compensation mechanism. In this way, the estimator preserves the physical interpretability of the model-based observer while accounting for the dominant systematic component of the voltage residual. For the baseline Single-EKF state estimator, the discrete-time prediction model is written as 𝐱 ^ k − \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-} = A d ​ ( T k ) ​ 𝐱 ^ k − 1 + B d ​ ( T k ) ​ I k , \displaystyle=A_{d}(T_{k})\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1}+B_{d}(T_{k})I_{k}, (23) P k − \displaystyle P_{k}^{-} = A d ​ ( T k ) ​ P k − 1 ​ A d ⊤ ​ ( T k ) + Q x , \displaystyle=A_{d}(T_{k})P_{k-1}A_{d}^{\top}(T_{k})+Q_{x}, (24) where 𝐱 ^ k − \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-} and P k − P_{k}^{-} are the a priori state estimate and covariance matrix, respectively, and Q x Q_{x} denotes the state process noise covariance. Without residual-bias compensation, the predicted terminal voltage is z ^ k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ k − , I k , T k ) , \hat{z}_{k}=h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-},I_{k},T_{k}), (25) and the corresponding innovation is e k = z k − z ^ k . e_{k}=z_{k}-\hat{z}_{k}. (26) Using the linearized observation matrix H x , k = ∂ h ∂ 𝐱 | 𝐱 ^ k − , H_{x,k}=\left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-}}, (27) the Kalman gain is obtained as K k = P k − ​ H x , k ⊤ ​ ( H x , k ​ P k − ​ H x , k ⊤ + R x ) − 1 , K_{k}=P_{k}^{-}H_{x,k}^{\top}\left(H_{x,k}P_{k}^{-}H_{x,k}^{\top}+R_{x}\right)^{-1}, (28) where R x R_{x} is the measurement noise covariance. The posterior state update is then 𝐱 ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k} = 𝐱 ^ k − + K k ​ e k , \displaystyle=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-}+K_{k}e_{k}, (29) P k \displaystyle P_{k} = ( I − K k ​ H x , k ) ​ P k − ​ ( I − K k ​ H x , k ) ⊤ + K k ​ R x ​ K k ⊤ . \displaystyle=(I-K_{k}H_{x,k})P_{k}^{-}(I-K_{k}H_{x,k})^{\top}+K_{k}R_{x}K_{k}^{\top}. (30) Although this standard EKF can provide satisfactory SOC estimation under healthy sensing conditions, it becomes vulnerable when a systematic abnormal voltage deviation is present. In such cases, the innovation term mixes state-related model mismatch and fault-induced measurement deviation, so the filter tends to absorb these systematic residuals into the electrochemical state estimate, which eventually degrades SOC estimation accuracy. To accommodate this systematic discrepancy, a lumped voltage-discrepancy state is introduced into the observation equation. Let θ k \theta_{k} denote the dominant systematic component of the voltage residual to be estimated online, which may originate from sensor faults, model mismatch, or other unmodeled effects. The augmented observation model is then written as z k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 k , I k , T k ) + θ k + v k , z_{k}=h(\mathbf{x}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\theta_{k}+v_{k}, (31) where v k v_{k} is the measurement noise. In this formulation, sensor fault and model mismatch are not explicitly separated, but are absorbed into the lumped voltage-discrepancy state. Under this formulation, the electrochemical state observer remains responsible for tracking battery dynamics, while the voltage-discrepancy state captures the dominant systematic component of the voltage mismatch. Based on this augmented formulation, the proposed framework proceeds in two sequential steps at each sampling instant. Rather than augmenting the electrochemical states and the voltage-discrepancy term into a single higher-dimensional EKF, the proposed method updates them sequentially in two coupled EKF loops. This realization provides the modularity required here: state and residual adaptation retain separate covariance recursions and can be enabled at different times. A conventional joint EKF is included as the principal augmented-state baseline in Section 3.4 . Because both 𝐱 k \mathbf{x}_{k} and θ k \theta_{k} influence the same scalar voltage measurement, their contributions are not independently identifiable from a single measurement without additional structure. The electrochemical dynamics and scalar random walk regularize this allocation operationally, while the covariance settings determine the relative adaptation bandwidth. They do not establish source identifiability. First, the electrochemical state is updated using the current voltage-discrepancy estimate. At time step k k , the most recent available voltage-discrepancy estimate, namely θ ^ k − 1 \hat{\theta}_{k-1} , is used in the state-update loop. The a priori voltage prediction becomes z ^ k − = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ k − , I k , T k ) + θ ^ k − 1 . \hat{z}_{k}^{-}=h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-},I_{k},T_{k})+\hat{\theta}_{k-1}. (32) The Jacobian with respect to the electrochemical state remains H x , k = ∂ h ∂ 𝐱 | 𝐱 ^ k − . H_{x,k}=\left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-}}. (33) The state innovation, innovation covariance, and gain are given by e x , k \displaystyle e_{x,k} = z k − z ^ k − , \displaystyle=z_{k}-\hat{z}_{k}^{-}, (34) S x , k \displaystyle S_{x,k} = H x , k ​ P k − ​ H x , k ⊤ + R x , \displaystyle=H_{x,k}P_{k}^{-}H_{x,k}^{\top}+R_{x}, (35) K x , k \displaystyle K_{x,k} = P k − ​ H x , k ⊤ ​ S x , k − 1 . \displaystyle=P_{k}^{-}H_{x,k}^{\top}S_{x,k}^{-1}. (36) The posterior state update is 𝐱 ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k} = 𝐱 ^ k − + K x , k ​ e x , k , \displaystyle=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k}^{-}+K_{x,k}e_{x,k}, (37) P k \displaystyle P_{k} = ( I − K x , k ​ H x , k ) ​ P k − ​ ( I − K x , k ​ H x , k ) ⊤ + K x , k ​ R x ​ K x , k ⊤ . \displaystyle=(I-K_{x,k}H_{x,k})P_{k}^{-}(I-K_{x,k}H_{x,k})^{\top}+K_{x,k}R_{x}K_{x,k}^{\top}. (38) Second, after the electrochemical state has been corrected, the voltage-discrepancy state is updated using the remaining voltage residual. Its evolution is modeled as a random walk: θ k = θ k − 1 + w θ , k , \theta_{k}=\theta_{k-1}+w_{\theta,k}, (39) where w θ , k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Q θ ) w_{\theta,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{\theta}) . The random-walk model provides a flexible low-order stochastic description of an unknown systematic voltage discrepancy, while Q θ Q_{\theta} determines the available adaptation bandwidth. The prediction step for the voltage-discrepancy state is therefore θ ^ k − \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{k}^{-} = θ ^ k − 1 , \displaystyle=\hat{\theta}_{k-1}, (40) P θ , k − \displaystyle P_{\theta,k}^{-} = P θ , k − 1 + Q θ . \displaystyle=P_{\theta,k-1}+Q_{\theta}. (41) Using the updated state estimate, the compensated voltage prediction is z ^ θ , k = h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ k , I k , T k ) + θ ^ k − . \hat{z}_{\theta,k}=h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k},I_{k},T_{k})+\hat{\theta}_{k}^{-}. (42) Because the voltage-discrepancy term enters the observation model additively, the corresponding Jacobian is simply H θ , k = 1 . H_{\theta,k}=1. (43) The voltage-discrepancy innovation, innovation covariance, and gain are then e θ , k \displaystyle e_{\theta,k} = z k − z ^ θ , k , \displaystyle=z_{k}-\hat{z}_{\theta,k}, (44) S θ , k \displaystyle S_{\theta,k} = P θ , k − + R θ , \displaystyle=P_{\theta,k}^{-}+R_{\theta}, (45) K θ , k \displaystyle K_{\theta,k} = P θ , k − ​ S θ , k − 1 , \displaystyle=P_{\theta,k}^{-}S_{\theta,k}^{-1}, (46) and the posterior update is obtained as θ ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{k} = θ ^ k − + K θ , k ​ e θ , k , \displaystyle=\hat{\theta}_{k}^{-}+K_{\theta,k}e_{\theta,k}, (47) P θ , k \displaystyle P_{\theta,k} = ( 1 − K θ , k ) ​ P θ , k − ​ ( 1 − K θ , k ) ⊤ + K θ , k ​ R θ ​ K θ , k ⊤ . \displaystyle=(1-K_{\theta,k})P_{\theta,k}^{-}(1-K_{\theta,k})^{\top}+K_{\theta,k}R_{\theta}K_{\theta,k}^{\top}. (48) The estimated voltage-discrepancy state provides an auxiliary signal reflecting systematic voltage mismatch. Its interpretation and the information needed for fault-source isolation are discussed in Section 5.5 . This sequential structure constitutes the fixed-architecture RBC-DEKF. Its essential feature is the explicit functional separation of battery-state correction and systematic voltage-residual compensation: the electrochemical state estimator follows internal battery dynamics, whereas the voltage-discrepancy estimator adapts to the dominant systematic voltage deviation. Whether a particular innovation component is assigned to 𝐱 \mathbf{x} or θ \theta remains tuning- and excitation-dependent; Section 3.3 therefore adds a temporal constraint for uncertain initialization. In all main experiments, the voltage-discrepancy state is initialized without a preloaded correction: θ ^ 0 = 0 . \hat{\theta}_{0}=0. (49) The former first-residual warm start, θ ^ 0 = z 0 − h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 , I 0 , T 0 ) \hat{\theta}_{0}=z_{0}-h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0},I_{0},T_{0}) , is retained only as an initialization ablation in Section 4.2 . At each sampling instant, the proposed estimator follows the sequence: 1. predict the electrochemical state and covariance; 2. update the electrochemical state using the current voltage-discrepancy estimate; 3. predict the voltage-discrepancy state; 4. update the voltage-discrepancy state using the residual computed from the corrected state; 5. calculate SOC from the updated electrochemical state. Compared with the conventional Single-EKF, the fixed-architecture RBC-DEKF introduces only one additional scalar variable and its associated covariance update, while preserving the same electrochemical state-space model. This adds only a scalar recursion and is amenable to online implementation. For additive sensor faults, the estimated voltage-discrepancy term accommodates the combined discrepancy containing the measurement offset. For multiplicative gain faults, it recursively represents a combined residual containing α ​ V k true \alpha V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}} and systematic model discrepancy. Because both enter as a scalar voltage-domain quantity, a one-dimensional compensation state can represent their combined instantaneous effect without explicitly estimating α \alpha . The practical fit is governed by residual magnitude and temporal bandwidth and by the fixed covariance tuning of the residual loop.

sections.heading: 3.3 Commissioning under uncertain initial SOC
sections.text: When the initial SOC prior is reliable, the original RBC-DEKF is used directly. When the prior is declared uncertain and a healthy startup window is independently verified, commissioning temporarily suspends the voltage-discrepancy estimator, selects an electrochemically consistent initial state from the buffered measurements, and replays the corrected state before sequential residual accommodation begins. Figure 3 summarizes these three online stages. A frozen healthy-model calibration supports the procedure; its construction and ablation are given in B .

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Commissioning principle
sections.text: During a window of N c = W c / Δ ​ t N_{c}=W_{c}/\Delta t samples ( W c = 300 W_{c}=300 s and Δ ​ t = 1 \Delta t=1 s here), residual prediction and correction are disabled: θ ^ k = 0 , k = 0 , … , N c − 1 . \hat{\theta}_{k}=0,\qquad k=0,\ldots,N_{c}-1. (50) The four-state EKF remains active, producing causal provisional SOC estimates and buffering current, temperature, and voltage. The BMS supplies both the uncertain-prior and healthy-window flags; a sensor abnormality already present at startup is outside this protocol. A temperature-specific healthy-residual map δ ^ h , k \hat{\delta}_{h,k} is fitted offline using the other two drive cycles at the same temperature, excluding the target cycle from training. It predicts repeatable healthy-model voltage discrepancy from SOC and causal current-history features and is frozen during operation. Reference SOC is used for offline fitting; candidate or estimated SOC is used online. The calibration remains in the commissioned voltage prediction after handover and is distinct from the adaptive voltage-discrepancy state.

sections.heading: 3.3.3 Replay and handover
sections.text: The selected initial state is replayed through the buffered samples using the calibrated four-state EKF. Its terminal state and covariance become the handover condition. Earlier provisional outputs are retained; the replay endpoint is emitted when the window completes. From the next sample, the scalar residual EKF starts from zero with the original Q θ Q_{\theta} , R θ R_{\theta} , and P θ , 0 P_{\theta,0} settings. The frozen calibration remains in both measurement predictions. Retaining this calibration after handover keeps the measurement model consistent with state correction and replay, avoiding reintroduction of the repeatable healthy-model discrepancy at the commissioning boundary. The reactivated residual state accommodates deviations beyond the frozen prediction, including calibration error; these operational roles do not imply source separation. The 300-s window is a fixed interior point in the observed 180–600-s stable-correction range on the tested trajectories (Section 4.6.1 ). Hereafter, commissioned RBC-DEKF denotes this complete calibrated realization. The contribution of this calibration is quantified by the ablation in B . sections.heading: 3.6 Filter settings and implementation details
sections.text: Separate covariance settings are assigned to the electrochemical state estimator and the voltage-discrepancy loop. For the state estimator, the process noise covariance is set to Q x = 10 − 18 ​ I 4 , Q_{x}=10^{-18}I_{4}, (70) the measurement noise covariance is R x = 10 − 5 , R_{x}=10^{-5}, (71) and the initial state covariance is P x , 0 = 10 − 6 ​ I 4 . P_{x,0}=10^{-6}I_{4}. (72) The very small Q x Q_{x} makes the recursive state estimate rely primarily on model propagation, initialization, and the limited voltage correction available on the LFP plateau. It is reported as a design setting rather than interpreted as a measured physical process-noise variance. For the voltage-discrepancy loop, the process noise, measurement noise, and initial covariance are chosen as Q θ \displaystyle Q_{\theta} = 5 × 10 − 3 , \displaystyle=5\times 10^{-3}, (73) R θ \displaystyle R_{\theta} = 3 × 10 − 4 , \displaystyle=3\times 10^{-4}, (74) P θ , 0 \displaystyle P_{\theta,0} = 3 × 10 3 . \displaystyle=3\times 10^{3}. (75) These covariance values were selected empirically and kept fixed for all operating conditions and fault levels. The large initial covariance enables rapid early-stage adaptation, while Q θ Q_{\theta} provides sufficient responsiveness to systematic voltage deviations and R θ R_{\theta} regularizes the update against measurement noise. The voltage-related covariance quantities R x R_{x} , Q θ Q_{\theta} , R θ R_{\theta} , and P θ , 0 P_{\theta,0} are expressed in V 2 \mathrm{V}^{2} . These quantities are filter-design covariances rather than direct estimates of the injected sensor-noise variance. The Jacobian of the nonlinear voltage model with respect to the four electrochemical states is evaluated by forward finite differences with a state perturbation of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , whereas the Jacobian with respect to the additive voltage-discrepancy state is exactly one. The covariance matrices are updated using the Joseph form for improved numerical robustness. The initial electrochemical state is constructed from the initial SOC estimate by mapping the cell-level SOC to the average concentrations of both electrodes and setting each initial surface concentration equal to the corresponding average concentration, which represents a uniform initial concentration profile within the solid particles.

sections.text: The robustness of the original RBC-DEKF was further evaluated across wide temperature variation and different dynamic drive cycles under additive and multiplicative voltage abnormalities. To provide both condition-map and aggregated-trend perspectives, the analysis is presented in two complementary forms. Figure 7 uses SOC-RMSE heatmaps to show how the error distribution changes jointly with temperature and fault magnitude for both the Single-EKF and the original RBC-DEKF. Figure 8 then summarizes the corresponding trends across fault levels, temperatures, and drive cycles using grouped curves. The associated numerical results are reported in Tables 12 and 13 . For additive bias faults, Figure 7 (a)–(b) show that the RBC-DEKF keeps SOC RMSE below 0.7 pp throughout the tested temperature–fault plane; most points are at or below 0.1 pp above 10 ∘ ​ C 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C} , whereas the Single-EKF error increases sharply with bias magnitude. The aggregated results in Figure 8 (a), (c), and (e) and Table 12 show the same trend. Under + 30 +30 mV bias, compensated SOC RMSE remains below 0.51 pp at every temperature and below 0.1 pp from 20 ∘ ​ C 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C} upward. The cycle-wise means are 0.155, 0.119, and 0.174 pp under DST, FUDS, and US06, respectively. Under gain faults, Figure 7 (c)–(d) show low RBC-DEKF error over most of the tested plane. At + 3 % +3\% gain, SOC RMSE reaches 4.604 pp at 20 ∘ ​ C 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C} but remains at or below 1.398 pp at the other temperatures. This case corresponds to an average equivalent residual near 95 mV, substantially beyond the 30 mV additive-bias range. The aggregated fault-level and cycle-dependent trends in Figure 8 (b), (d), and (f) further clarify this result. At 25 ∘ ​ C 25^{\circ}\mathrm{C} , the original RBC-DEKF remains accurate over moderate gain levels and shows increased error mainly under the most severe positive gain condition. The temperature-dependent comparison in Figure 8 (d) confirms that the remaining error is concentrated in a limited set of operating conditions rather than distributed across the full thermal range. In the voltage-residual domain, the fixed random-walk loop must track an equivalent residual whose amplitude and temporal variation both increase with the gain level and the terminal-voltage trajectory. For + 3 % +3\% gain, the compensated SOC RMSE is 0.220, 0.403, and 3.161 pp under DST, FUDS, and US06, respectively. Additive-bias performance remains nearly invariant over the test matrix. Gain-fault performance is also close to the nominal estimation level in most conditions, with the remaining errors concentrated at the largest equivalent-residual magnitude and the most demanding operating profiles. sections.heading: 5.1 Why a dual realization: functional decoupling versus joint augmentation
sections.text: The conventional joint-EKF baseline propagates the full cross covariance and is more accurate on average than the original RBC-DEKF under accurate initialization and the inherited covariance values (0.092811 versus 0.251308 percentage points over all 384 static condition–fault profiles). Under accurate initialization, when electrochemical-state errors are small, the remaining voltage innovation can be dominated by the lumped voltage discrepancy rather than a genuine SOC mismatch. In this regime, the Joint-EKF uses the propagated residual-state uncertainty and state–residual cross covariance within one common augmented update [Eqs. ( 66 )–( 67 )], which can moderate unnecessary electrochemical-state correction. By contrast, the sequential RBC-DEKF first updates the electrochemical state using a gain that does not directly contain P θ , k − P_{\theta,k}^{-} [Eq. ( 63 )], and only afterward updates the voltage-discrepancy state using the same voltage sample. Consequently, part of a discrepancy-dominated innovation can enter the electrochemical-state correction before the residual loop adapts. This provides a first-order mechanism consistent with the lower Joint-EKF SOC RMSE observed under accurate initialization. Because the two realizations also use different measurement-weighting structures and inherited covariance tuning, the observed performance difference is not attributed to cross-covariance propagation alone. The dual realization instead maintains separate state and residual design covariances, so P θ , k − P_{\theta,k}^{-} does not directly change K x , k D K_{x,k}^{D} and the scalar residual recursion can be suspended while the four-state Joseph covariance update is retained. This functional decoupling enables the commissioning procedure while retaining the four-state EKF recursion structure. In the representative + 10 +10 -percentage-point case of Figure 10 , the two always-on residual-state estimators retain errors near 10 percentage points, whereas the complete commissioned realization attains a post-handover SOC RMSE of 0.671 percentage points. The result supports the combined startup procedure—including bounded state correction and frozen healthy-residual calibration—rather than a universal numerical ranking of dual and joint filters.

sections.heading: 5.2 Initial-state uncertainty and intrinsic observability
sections.text: On the flat plateau, the local startup innovation has the schematic form ν k ≃ h s ​ δ ​ SOC k + δ ​ θ k + v k , \nu_{k}\simeq h_{s}\,\delta\mathrm{SOC}_{k}+\delta\theta_{k}+v_{k}, (84) with small | h s | |h_{s}| . Adding θ \theta does not increase | h s | |h_{s}| , add a sensor, or create intrinsic SOC observability. It instead adds another explanation for the same innovation and can therefore preserve an initial SOC error when the residual loop adapts rapidly. Commissioning temporarily imposes the verified-healthy constraint θ = 0 \theta=0 and restricts the startup correction to the model-generated, SOC-aligned trajectories defined in Section 3.3 . The window objective combines these trajectories with the disclosed frozen healthy-residual calibration; it does not add an online measurement channel or guarantee unique physical-state recovery. If a voltage fault is already present at sample zero, or if the healthy model discrepancy is inadequately calibrated, the two contributions remain non-identifiable from this single voltage channel. The proposed procedure must therefore be viewed as conditional state recovery under a healthy-window assumption. The commissioning correction acts on the electrochemical state coordinates rather than directly resetting scalar SOC. Equation ( 51 ) follows the two-electrode stoichiometric mapping of Eq. ( 11 ); in the 50%-SOC-anchored tests, the initial perturbation and candidate correction use the same SOC-aligned direction while retaining the checkpoint’s pre-existing dynamic profile information. Each candidate is propagated over the measured current–temperature window and ranked by the full calibrated terminal-voltage prediction, which combines both electrode OCPs with diffusion, kinetic, and ohmic terms. The result is a paired-electrode, model-constrained initialization rather than inversion of a scalar OCV–SOC curve. Although the quasi-equilibrium full-cell OCV slope is small on the LFP plateau, the commissioning objective uses a finite current-driven trajectory rather than a single voltage sample. SOC-aligned candidates generate different paired-electrode concentration trajectories, whose concentration-dependent OCP and kinetic contributions can produce different terminal-voltage predictions over the buffered window. Accumulating these voltage-consistency differences helps rank candidate initial states under the verified-healthy assumption. The available trajectory and model calibration determine the usefulness of this comparison; the procedure does not create new instantaneous SOC observability.

sections.heading: 5.3 Equivalent-residual interpretation of multiplicative gain faults
sections.text: The gain-fault results can be interpreted most clearly in the voltage-residual domain. For a constant gain coefficient α \alpha , the induced residual is b k gain = α ​ V k true . b_{k}^{\mathrm{gain}}=\alpha V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}. (85) By decomposing the true terminal voltage as V k true = V ¯ true + V ~ k true V_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}=\overline{V}^{\mathrm{true}}+\widetilde{V}_{k}^{\mathrm{true}} , the equivalent residual becomes b k gain = α ​ V ¯ true + α ​ V ~ k true . b_{k}^{\mathrm{gain}}=\alpha\overline{V}^{\mathrm{true}}+\alpha\widetilde{V}_{k}^{\mathrm{true}}. (86) The first term represents the mean voltage-domain offset, whereas the second describes its variation with terminal voltage. The voltage-discrepancy state estimates the combined systematic voltage discrepancy, including the gain-induced residual and model mismatch. Therefore, although the RBC-DEKF does not identify the gain coefficient α \alpha explicitly, its scalar residual state can represent the instantaneous voltage-domain effect of the gain fault. The matched-magnitude results in Section 4.2 show similar accommodation of additive and gain faults when their equivalent voltage residuals are comparable. Remaining errors are concentrated where the gain-induced residual is larger and more time-varying than the tested additive offsets. The observed sign asymmetry indicates interaction with nonlinear voltage–state sensitivity and fixed covariance tuning. Explicit bias–gain estimation may be useful for fault-mode identification, while the present scalar state supports the reported voltage-domain accommodation.

sections.heading: 5.4 Implications for flat-plateau battery chemistries
sections.text: The results demonstrate that fault-tolerant state estimation cannot be considered independently of battery chemistry. In LFP batteries, the two-phase plateau weakens the mapping from terminal voltage to lithiation state, allowing systematic voltage abnormalities to dominate the voltage innovation used by a voltage-corrected observer. The RBC-DEKF provides a separate adaptive channel for the dominant systematic voltage discrepancy alongside the electrochemical state estimator. The underlying design principle may also be relevant to other flat-voltage or phase-transition-dominated electrode systems. However, the quantitative compensation performance remains chemistry dependent because it is governed by the local voltage–composition slope, dynamic polarization, hysteresis, and model fidelity. Extension to other chemistries therefore requires chemistry-specific parameterization and independent validation rather than direct transfer of the numerical results reported here.

sections.heading: 5.5 Model mismatch, hysteresis, and residual interpretation
sections.text: The estimated residual must be interpreted as θ k = θ sensor , k + δ model , k + δ hys , k + δ other , k , \theta_{k}=\theta_{\mathrm{sensor},k}+\delta_{\mathrm{model},k}+\delta_{\mathrm{hys},k}+\delta_{\mathrm{other},k}, (87) not as a source-isolated sensor bias. Averaging low-rate charge and discharge OCV branches reduces first-order branch separation in the material-sensitivity plot, but does not remove dynamic hysteresis. The CPG-SPMT represents diffusion, charge-transfer polarization, ohmic loss, and temperature-dependent grouped parameters; it does not contain an explicit hysteresis state. Hysteresis, relaxation not captured by the reduced dynamics, parameter error, and voltage-sensor abnormality can consequently enter the same scalar residual. This distinction also changes the interpretation of voltage RMSE. A small posterior measurement-fit error shows that the augmented output can reconstruct the faulty sample after using that sample for correction. It is not evidence that the clean terminal voltage or physical sensor bias has been recovered. Source isolation would require additional information, such as redundant sensors, an explicit validated hysteresis model, fault-specific dynamics, or an independently calibrated healthy-residual envelope.

sections.heading: 5.6 Practical implications and future extensions
sections.text: From a battery-management perspective, the results show that a one-state voltage-discrepancy loop can improve the robustness of electrochemical-model-based SOC estimation under the tested additive-bias and multiplicative-gain voltage abnormalities without relying on sensor redundancy or SOC-region partitioning. This is particularly relevant to LFP batteries, for which the flat OCV response amplifies small voltage errors into large SOC ambiguity. The online voltage-discrepancy recursion adds only one scalar state; the uncertain-start branch additionally uses the disclosed offline calibration and finite-window commissioning procedure. Explicit fault-parameter identification is not required for the reported voltage-domain accommodation; embedded resource use remains to be measured. The explicit estimate θ ^ k \hat{\theta}_{k} may provide a candidate online abnormality signal. Because the estimated quantity is lumped, however, it does not by itself establish a sensor fault, isolate sensor effects from model mismatch, or classify additive and multiplicative modes. Reliable diagnostic decisions require a separately validated healthy residual baseline, adaptive thresholds, or an additional classification layer. A further limitation is that the present validation uses synthetically imposed measurement abnormalities on an open-source dataset; dedicated hardware experiments are required to quantify actual sensor drift, calibration errors, communication latency, and embedded implementation constraints. The present evidence has five practical boundaries. First, the voltage abnormalities are synthetic, the delayed profiles are representative accommodation tests rather than a detection benchmark, and autonomous fault classification is not validated. Second, the model and estimator assume a fixed health state. Aging, capacity fade, resistance growth, and state-of-health adaptation are outside the reported results. Third, current-sensor bias and joint current/voltage faults are not evaluated. Fourth, the commissioning study uses three representative 50%-SOC-anchored trajectories, one noise realization, and a supervised cross-cycle healthy-residual map; its repeated initial offsets are paired sensitivity cases rather than independent cells. Fifth, because all 24 temperature–cycle trajectories participate in parameter identification and/or candidate selection, the full static-fault matrix measures in-matrix operating-condition coverage rather than out-of-sample generalization. Future work should therefore combine explicit hysteresis and aging-aware electrochemical dynamics with capacity/SOH estimation; assess parameter mismatch and current-sensor bias; validate the uncertain-start commissioning decision on independent healthy cells; develop and validate a separate sensor-fault decision layer; and test physical sensor faults in hardware-in-the-loop and embedded BMS implementations. Joint bias–gain states may also be useful when direct fault-mode identification is required rather than voltage-domain accommodation alone.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This work developed an electrochemically constrained RBC-DEKF for accurate LFP SOC estimation under abnormal voltage measurements and uncertain initialization. The CPG-SPMT supplies paired-electrode concentration dynamics, while a separately configurable scalar residual loop accommodates the lumped systematic voltage discrepancy. Across 24 temperature–drive-cycle trajectories, the RBC-DEKF reduced mean SOC RMSE from 7.646 to 0.170 percentage points over 216 additive-bias profiles and from 22.646 to 0.356 percentage points over 168 multiplicative-gain profiles. For uncertain initialization, commissioning suspends the residual estimator, corrects paired-electrode initial states using buffered healthy data, and replays the calibrated state EKF before handover. Across 18 paired nonzero-initial-error profiles on three 50%-SOC-anchored segments, full-record mean SOC RMSE was 1.747 pp, including the startup transient, compared with 11.192 and 11.400 pp for the always-on RBC-DEKF and conventional joint EKF. Correction accuracy was stable over the tested 180–600-s windows, supporting the retained 300-s setting. Representative delayed step, 10-s ramp, and gain tests yielded post-fault RMSE values of 0.697–0.715 pp. The central novelty is the electrochemically constrained temporal coordination of uncertain-state recovery and subsequent voltage-discrepancy accommodation: the residual channel is suspended while an SOC-aligned, physically consistent paired-electrode state is selected from a verified-healthy trajectory, after which residual adaptation is reactivated for fault-tolerant operation. The reported commissioned accuracy belongs to the complete realization, including the frozen healthy-model calibration. Physical sensor-fault validation, aging-aware calibration, and fault-source classification remain directions for further work.

Affiliation: Institute for Materials Research (IUMAT), Hasselt University, Martelarenlaan 42, Hasselt, 3500, Belgium Affiliation: EnergyVille, Thor Park 8310, Genk, 3600, Belgium Abstract The flat voltage plateau of lithium iron phosphate (LFP)/graphite cells makes electrochemical-state errors and voltage-measurement abnormalities produce similar innovations, complicating state-of-charge (SOC) estimation. This work proposes an electrochemically constrained residual-bias compensation dual extended Kalman filter (RBC-DEKF) with uncertain-initialization commissioning. A thermal control-oriented parameter-grouped single-particle model (CPG-SPMT) provides paired-electrode dynamics and terminal-voltage prediction, while a separately configurable voltage-discrepancy state accommodates systematic residuals. When the initial SOC is uncertain, residual adaptation is suspended over a verified-healthy startup window. Buffered data support electrochemically constrained trajectory matching, followed by calibrated state replay and residual-channel reactivation. Frozen cross-cycle healthy-residual calibration supports commissioning and remains in the voltage prediction after handover. Evaluation covers 216 additive-bias and 168 multiplicative-gain profiles over 24 A123 temperature–drive-cycle trajectories. Relative to Single-EKF, the original RBC-DEKF reduces mean SOC RMSE from 7.646 to 0.170 percentage points for additive bias and from 22.646 to 0.356 percentage points for gain faults. Separately, 18 nonzero-initial-error profiles on three representative 50%-SOC-anchored segments give a full-record mean SOC RMSE of 1.747 percentage points, including startup, for the commissioned realization, versus 11.192 and 11.400 for the always-on RBC-DEKF and conventional joint EKF. Representative delayed bias, 10-s ramp, and gain tests show that the corrected SOC trajectory remains stable after fault introduction. The central contribution is electrochemically constrained temporal coordination of uncertain-state recovery and subsequent voltage-discrepancy accommodation. Keywords: Lithium iron phosphate , Flat voltage plateau , State-of-charge estimation , Electrochemical model , Voltage-fault accommodation , Uncertain-SOC commissioning 1 Introduction Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) has become one of the most widely deployed cathode materials in lithium-ion batteries for electric transportation and stationary energy-storage applications, owing to its intrinsic safety, long cycle life, thermal stability, and cost-effectiveness [ 28 , 25 , 16 ] . Despite these advantages, reliable state estimation remains particularly challenging for LFP batteries [ 23 , 41 ] . Lithium insertion and extraction proceed through a two-phase reaction between Li-rich LiFePO 4 and Li-poor FePO 4 , producing an extended and nearly flat open-circuit-voltage (OCV) plateau over a broad state-of-charge (SOC) range [ 6 , 51 ] . Within this plateau, the terminal voltage changes only weakly with SOC, substantially reducing voltage-based state observability [ 24 , 51 ] . Consequently, a small voltage uncertainty can correspond to a large SOC ambiguity, making voltage-corrected SOC estimation intrinsically more difficult for LFP batteries than for chemistries with steeper OCV–SOC characteristics. This weak observability places stringent requirements on the accuracy and reliability of voltage measurements used by battery management systems (BMSs) [ 27 , 32 , 4 , 51 ] . In long-term operation, however, voltage sensors may suffer from calibration drift, reference instability, component aging, and environmental influences [ 53 , 37 , 48 , 34 ] , with recent studies further emphasizing sensor-enabled monitoring under extreme environments and coupled thermal–electrical aging stresses [ 42 , 36 ] . These abnormalities commonly appear as additive offsets at the millivolt level or as multiplicative gain errors that rescale the measured voltage [ 54 ] . In an LFP battery, such apparently small sensing errors can be mapped onto disproportionately large corrections of the weakly observable electrochemical states, leading to severe SOC-estimation degradation or loss of convergence. Since SOC is a central variable for power limitation, energy management, balancing, and safety supervision, the resulting error can propagate through multiple BMS functions and compromise system-level reliability [ 31 , 46 ] . Voltage-sensor robustness is therefore not merely an instrumentation issue, but a material-dependent state-estimation problem for flat-plateau LFP batteries. Battery fault-diagnosis methods are commonly divided into signal-processing-based, data-driven, and model-based approaches. Signal-processing methods extract abnormal temporal or spectral features directly from measurements and are attractive because of their relatively simple implementation [ 50 , 47 ] . Their performance, however, can be sensitive to measurement noise, operating-condition variation, and the choice of diagnostic thresholds. Data-driven methods have demonstrated strong nonlinear representation capability for voltage-abnormality detection and battery fault classification [ 56 , 20 , 21 ] , but generally require representative fault data and may exhibit limited generalization to previously unseen cells, temperatures, and load profiles [ 55 , 18 , 43 ] . Recent realistic and model-constrained learning studies have improved fault diagnosis under stochastic and heterogeneous operating conditions [ 49 , 2 ] ; nevertheless, transferring laboratory-trained diagnosis models to practical battery systems remains difficult because of changing operating distributions, sensing limitations, and multi-scale fault manifestations [ 55 ] . Model-based approaches provide an alternative route by linking faults to the inconsistency between measured and model-predicted battery responses [ 44 , 5 ] ; structural residual analysis has also been developed to isolate concurrent electro–thermal faults in battery systems [ 33 ] . Most existing methods employ equivalent circuit models (ECMs), whose low computational cost and simple calibration are attractive for online BMS implementation. However, their residuals combine sensor abnormalities with process disturbances, parameter errors, and structural model mismatch, which complicates fault interpretation and threshold design [ 44 ] . This problem is particularly severe for LFP batteries: within the flat OCV region, a persistent voltage residual can be incorrectly explained by a large change in SOC even when the actual source is a sensor fault or modeling error. Electrochemical models offer a more physically consistent basis for separating voltage formation from internal-state evolution. The pseudo-two-dimensional model and its reduced-order variants explicitly represent lithium transport, interfacial kinetics, and electrode thermodynamics, thereby connecting terminal voltage to physically meaningful internal states [ 7 , 15 ] . Although the full-order model is generally too computationally demanding for recursive onboard estimation, reduced-order models such as the single-particle model preserve the dominant electrochemical dynamics at substantially lower computational cost [ 12 , 8 ] . A direct comparison on graphite/LFP cells reported an average voltage-prediction error of 51.5 mV for an ECM and 19.3 mV for a physics-based model over temperatures of 10–40 ∘ C and rates of C/3–2C, illustrating the value of electrochemical descriptions for LFP voltage prediction [ 19 ] . Residual correction provides an additional mechanism for addressing the discrepancy that remains even with a physics-based model. Physics-guided residual-learning frameworks have shown that an electrochemical-model prior can be combined with learned correction terms to improve LFP SOC estimation over broad temperature ranges and dynamic operating conditions [ 10 , 3 ] . These studies demonstrate that model residuals contain useful information for correcting state estimates. However, learned residual models generally require representative offline training data and primarily target model-induced prediction errors. They do not explicitly formulate voltage-sensor bias and gain abnormalities within the measurement model or recursively estimate a voltage-discrepancy state for online accommodation of both fault forms. Several fault-tolerant strategies more directly related to voltage measurements have also been investigated. Sensor-topology-based reconstruction can tolerate isolated voltage-sensor faults by exploiting redundant pack measurements [ 38 ] , but its applicability depends on measurement redundancy and fault configuration. Adaptive filtering can improve robustness against small voltage perturbations [ 22 ] , although such perturbations are often treated as generic uncertainty rather than explicit sensor faults. For LFP batteries, region-dependent methods have adjusted the correction strategy according to the local OCV slope or selected different observers for different OCV ranges [ 40 , 26 ] . Bias-compensated SOC and state-of-health estimation has also been developed by exploiting transitions between OCV regions [ 45 ] . These approaches improve estimation within flat-voltage regions, but typically require SOC-region identification, observer switching, or convergence across multiple charge–discharge intervals. In parallel, additive bias and multiplicative gain faults have been jointly represented through state augmentation in ECM-based estimators [ 54 ] . Their performance nevertheless remains strongly dependent on model fidelity and excitation, while the interaction between voltage-sensor abnormalities and the material-specific weak observability of LFP electrochemical states has not been explicitly addressed. Incorrect SOC initialization has been addressed through several complementary estimation strategies. Closed-loop UKF estimation has demonstrated self-correction from a large initial offset in an LFP cell [ 17 ] , while nonlinear observers have provided convergence analysis and recovery tests under a 20-percentage-point initial error [ 39 ] . Moving-horizon estimation exploits a finite measurement history and physical constraints to reduce sensitivity to mismatched initial conditions [ 29 , 30 ] , and adaptive robust filters improve convergence when the initial SOC, model parameters, and noise statistics are simultaneously uncertain [ 35 ] . These studies demonstrate the value of temporal excitation and constrained state evolution for recovering an uncertain SOC prior. Staged adaptation has also been used in battery state–parameter co-estimation. Voltage-error dead zones can temporarily suspend physical-parameter updates when the innovation is unsuitable for reliable adaptation, including during large SOC-initialization errors [ 14 ] . Such methods primarily regulate physical quantities such as capacity, impedance, or OCV-related coefficients. In the present fault-tolerant setting, the auxiliary state instead represents a voltage-domain discrepancy that must remain available for subsequent voltage-abnormality accommodation. Without a dedicated startup allocation strategy, this rapidly adaptive residual state can absorb an initial electrochemical-state mismatch and prevent SOC recovery. These studies highlight a central design challenge: on the flat LFP plateau, electrochemical-state error, model discrepancy, and sensor abnormality can produce similar voltage innovations. A fault-tolerant estimator must therefore coordinate state recovery and voltage-discrepancy accommodation without allowing a rapidly adaptive residual state to absorb uncertain initialization. Motivated by these considerations, this work develops an electrochemically constrained, commissioning-enabled fault-tolerant SOC-estimation framework for flat-plateau LFP batteries. The main contributions are threefold: 1. Material-specific fault sensitivity. The voltage-error sensitivity of LFP SOC estimation is quantified by linking the flat full-cell OCV response with the paired-electrode electrochemical description. This establishes the material-level motivation for explicitly accommodating systematic voltage discrepancy in flat-plateau state estimation. 2. Commissioning-enabled state–residual coordination. A sequential residual-bias compensation dual extended Kalman filter (RBC-DEKF) is developed with separately configurable electrochemical-state and voltage-discrepancy recursions. Under uncertain initialization, residual adaptation is temporarily suspended while an electrochemically consistent paired-electrode state is corrected from a verified-healthy buffered startup trajectory, after which residual accommodation is reactivated. 3. Systematic evaluation and operating-boundary analysis. Additive-bias and multiplicative-gain accommodation is evaluated over 24 temperature–drive-cycle trajectories, with separate representative tests of large initial-SOC errors and abnormalities introduced during operation. Comparisons with Single-EKF, open-loop propagation, and conventional joint augmentation distinguish fault accommodation from model propagation and state-recovery capability. 2 Electrochemical and material basis for state estimation 2.1 Classical SPM foundation The electrochemical backbone adopted in this work is derived from the classical SPM, which captures the essential solid-phase diffusion and interfacial-reaction dynamics in the negative and positive electrodes while remaining substantially simpler than full P2D formulations. In the classical SPM, solid-state lithium diffusion within representative spherical particles is governed by Fick’s law. The terminal voltage is obtained from the electrode open-circuit potentials together with charge-transfer overpotentials and lumped ohmic loss.
